memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text:
"During the night Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, 'Up! Leave my
people, you and the Israelites! Go, worship the LORD as you have requested. Take
your flocks and herds, as you have said, and go. And also bless me.'"
- Ex 12:31-32 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
The man who once demanded, "Who is the LORD, that I should obey him?" (Ex 5:2)
now stands in the dark and says, "Go... and also bless me."

Everything he had refused, he now gives. The people, the flocks, the herds, all
of it, without conditions. And then that strange final plea: bless me also.

It is worth pausing there. Is this repentance? It does not seem to be. Within
days Pharaoh will change his mind again and chase them to the sea. This looks
like the cry of a man broken by consequences rather than changed in heart. Paul
distinguishes "godly sorrow" that brings repentance from "worldly sorrow" that
brings death (2 Cor 7:10). One turns to God. The other only wants the pain to
stop.

That is a searching distinction for us. It is possible to weep over the results
of our sin without ever turning from the sin itself. Real repentance is not
measured by how badly we feel at midnight, but by what we do at daybreak.

Yet notice: even here, Pharaoh knew where blessing came from. Some part of him
recognised the God he had defied.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. When you have been sorry, was it for the sin or for the consequences?
2. What would genuine turning look like in your life this week?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text:
Lord, give me godly sorrow that leads to real change, not just regret over
consequences. Turn my heart, not only my feelings. Amen.
